glosses: Real or perceived movement of atmospheric air usually caused by convection or differences in air pressure.

examples.text: The wind blew through her hair as she stood on the deck of the ship.
As they accelerated onto the motorway, the wind tore the plywood off the car's roof-rack.
The winds in Chicago are fierce.
There was a sudden gust of wind, on which spores were borne away.
The window was banging in the wind.

Since the mid-1980s, when Indonesia first began to clear its bountiful forests on an industrial scale in favour of lucrative palm-oil plantations, “haze” has become an almost annual occurrence in South-East Asia. The cheapest way to clear logged woodland is to burn it, producing an acrid cloud of foul white smoke that, carried by the wind, can cover hundreds, or even thousands, of square miles.

glosses: Air artificially put in motion by any force or action.

examples.text: the wind of a cannon ball
the wind of a bellows

glosses: The ability to breathe easily.

examples.text: After the second lap he was already out of wind.
The fall knocked the wind out of him.

glosses: News of an event, especially by hearsay or gossip.

examples.text: to catch wind of something
Steve caught wind of Martha's dalliance with his best friend.
Police got wind of the lottery, tried to track it down.

glosses: A tendency or trend.

examples.text: the wind of change
But many of those issues failed to draw Spanish voters, or even scared them, and the country’s election results went contrary to Europe’s political winds.

glosses: One of the four elements of the ancient Greeks and Romans; air.
One of the five basic elements in Indian and Japanese models of the Classical elements.
Flatus.

examples.text: to pass wind

glosses: Breath modulated by the respiratory and vocal organs, or by an instrument.

examples.text: Their instruments were various in their kind, / Some for the bow, and some for breathing wind.

glosses: The woodwind section of an orchestra. Occasionally also used to include the brass section.
A woodwind instrument. Occasionally also used to describe a brass instrument.
A direction from which the wind may blow; a point of the compass; especially, one of the cardinal points.

examples.text: the four winds
Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain.

When this conversation was repeated in detail within the hearing of the young woman in question, and undoubtedly for his benefit, Mr. Trevor threw shame to the winds and scandalized the Misses Brewster then and there by proclaiming his father to have been a country storekeeper.

glosses: Types of playing-tile in the game of mah-jongg, named after the four winds.
A disease of sheep, in which the intestines are distended with air, or rather affected with a violent inflammation. It occurs immediately after shearing.
Mere breath or talk; empty effort; idle words.

examples.text: Nor think thou with wind / Of airy threats to awe.
Political language is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable, and to give an appearance of solidity to pure wind.

glosses: A bird, the dotterel.
The region of the solar plexus, where a blow may paralyze the diaphragm and cause temporary loss of breath or other injury.
To blow air through a wind instrument or horn to make a sound.

examples.text: Earl Walter winds his bugle horn; / To horſe, to horſe, halloo, halloo! / His fiery courſer ſnuffs the morn, / And thronging ſerfs their Lord purſue.
Something higher must lie at the back of that eager response to pack-music and winded horn — something born of the smell of the good earth

glosses: To cause (someone) to become breathless, as by a blow to the abdomen, or by physical exertion, running, etc.

examples.text: The boxer was winded during round two.

glosses: To cause a baby to bring up wind by patting its back after being fed.
To turn a boat or ship around, so that the wind strikes it on the opposite side.
To expose to the wind; to winnow; to ventilate.
To perceive or follow by scent.

examples.text: The hounds winded the game.

glosses: To rest (a horse, etc.) in order to allow the breath to be recovered; to breathe.
To turn a windmill so that its sails face into the wind.
To turn coils of (a cord or something similar) around something.

examples.text: to wind thread on a spool or into a ball
Whether to wind / The woodbine round this arbour.

It was April 22, 1831, and a young man was walking down Whitehall in the direction of Parliament Street. He wore shepherd's plaid trousers and the swallow-tail coat of the day, with a figured muslin cravat wound about his wide-spread collar.

glosses: To tighten the spring of a clockwork mechanism.

examples.text: Please wind that old-fashioned alarm clock.

glosses: To entwist; to enfold; to encircle.

examples.text: Sleep, and I will wind thee in arms.

glosses: To travel or follow a path with numerous curves.

examples.text: Vines wind round a pole.  The river winds through the plain.

The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea.

The long and winding road / That leads to your door / Will never disappear.

glosses: To have complete control over; to turn and bend at one's pleasure; to vary or alter at will; to regulate; to govern.

examples.text: to turn and wind a fiery Pegasus

glosses: To introduce by insinuation; to insinuate.

examples.text: You have contrived[…]to wind / Yourself into a power tyrannical.

glosses: To cover or surround with something coiled about.

examples.text: to wind a rope with twine

glosses: To cause to move by exerting a winding force; to haul or hoist as by a winch.

examples.text: Quickly she slammed the door shut and panicking wound the window up as fast as her slippery fingers would allow.

glosses: To turn (a ship) around, end for end.
The act of winding or turning; a turn; a bend; a twist.
